opus-5.5.text:
I think blueprints are one of the most underrated pieces of infrastructure in formalization. When people picture a big formalization project, they often imagine a lone genius sitting with Lean, translating a proof line by line. The reality of something like the Polynomial Freiman–Ruzsa project or the Fermat's Last Theorem effort that Kevin Buzzard is leading is much more like a construction site, and a blueprint is literally what it sounds like: the architectural drawing everyone works from.

Concretely, a blueprint takes an informal proof and breaks it into a dependency graph of small statements: definitions, lemmas, theorems. Each node is written in human-readable mathematics, and each one is linked to its formal counterpart in Lean. The graph is color-coded, so you can see at a glance what's been stated, what's been proved, and what's ready to be worked on because all of its dependencies are done. That turns one enormous, intimidating task into hundreds of bite-sized, well-specified ones.

That decomposition does a few important things. First, it makes parallelism possible. Terence Tao has talked about how in the PFR project, people he'd never met could pick up a single lemma, formalize it, and contribute, without understanding the entire argument. The blueprint acts as a contract: if you prove this statement exactly as specified, it'll slot into the whole. That's very similar to how large software projects work with interfaces and modules.

Second, it separates two kinds of expertise. The person who deeply understands the mathematics can write the blueprint, and someone who's very fluent in Lean and Mathlib, but maybe not an expert in that particular field, can do the formalization. That lowers the barrier to entry a lot.

Third, and this is something I find really interesting, the process of writing a blueprint often surfaces gaps in the informal proof. When you're forced to make every dependency explicit, you discover that a step the paper calls "obvious" actually requires a whole auxiliary lemma, or that some hypothesis was quietly assumed. So the blueprint isn't just a project management tool; it's a kind of intermediate level of rigor sitting between a traditional paper and fully formal code.

From the perspective of AI, which is what I think about a lot, blueprints are very exciting because they define exactly the right granularity for machines to help. Asking a model to formalize an entire research paper end to end is still very hard. But asking it to prove one well-scoped node in a dependency graph, with the surrounding context given, is much more tractable. So I see blueprints as a natural bridge: today they coordinate human collaborators, and increasingly they'll coordinate humans and AI systems working together, with AI eventually helping to generate the blueprints themselves, by taking an informal argument and proposing the decomposition. That's where I think the scaling of formal mathematics really starts to happen.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a blueprint breaks a project into small, specified lemmas and lets distributed contributors pick up and formalize individual lemmas.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the blueprint is actually one of the most underappreciated pieces of infrastructure in the whole formalization ecosystem, and it's the thing that made projects like the Liquid Tensor Experiment, or the sphere eversion project, or the Polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa formalization that Terry Tao ran, actually feasible as collaborative efforts.

Here's the basic problem. When you want to formalize a big result in Lean, the final proof might be tens of thousands of lines. No single person can hold the whole thing in their head, and no single person has the time to do it alone. So you need to parallelize. But a mathematical proof isn't naturally parallelizable the way, say, a large software project is, because every lemma depends on definitions and other lemmas, and if someone upstream changes a definition slightly, everything downstream can break.

The blueprint solves this by sitting in between the informal mathematics and the formal code. It's essentially a very carefully written human-readable document, usually in LaTeX, where the proof is broken down into a dependency graph of small statements. Each node is a lemma or a definition, written precisely enough that you know exactly what the Lean statement should be, and each node lists explicitly which other nodes it depends on. Patrick Massot built the tooling for this, and the output is this interactive graph where every node is colored by its status: has the statement been formalized, has the proof been formalized, is it fully checked.

What that does socially is really powerful. Someone can show up, look at the graph, find a leaf node that's green on the statement side but not on the proof side, and just claim it. They don't need to understand the whole project. They need to understand one lemma and its immediate neighbors. That's what let the PFR project go from announcement to fully formalized in about three weeks with dozens of contributors, many of whom had never spoken to Terry before.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that writing the blueprint is itself a mathematical act, and often the hardest part. You discover that the paper proof glossed over something, or that the "obvious" step actually requires a different hypothesis. A lot of the real intellectual work happens at the blueprint stage before anyone writes a line of Lean. In that sense the blueprint is where informal rigor gets converted into formal rigor, and it forces the mathematician to confront the gaps honestly.

And from the perspective of what we're building, this is very relevant to AI systems too. If you want a model to help with a large formalization, you can't just hand it a theorem statement and say "prove this." You want it to work at the level of the blueprint, decomposing, proposing lemma statements, filling in nodes, and the blueprint gives you a natural structure for that collaboration between humans and machines. The graph is a shared language.

r001.rationale: The response explains that contributors can use the blueprint graph to find and claim an individual lemma, without needing to understand the whole project.

astra-6.text:
I think of a blueprint as the bridge between a mathematical argument and its formal implementation. A paper is written for a human reader, who can fill in gaps and recognize which steps are routine. For a large formalization project, you want to make that structure much more explicit: what are the precise statements, which lemmas depend on which others, and how do they fit together to prove the main theorem?

That also makes the blueprint a coordination tool. People can work on different parts of the proof with a shared understanding of what each part needs to deliver. You don’t have to hold the entire project in your head to contribute meaningfully.

And I think the process goes both ways. Formalizing a proof can reveal a missing assumption or a step that needs more work, and that feeds back into the blueprint. So it’s a living mathematical plan. It helps turn a large proof into pieces that a team can work on and eventually assemble into a fully checked result.

r001.rationale: The response says people can work on different parts and contribute using a shared understanding, but it does not identify a mechanism for contributors to claim small tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think blueprints provide the bridge between a mathematical argument and its formalization. A paper is written for a human reader, who can fill in gaps or recognize that something follows from a standard result. In a formal proof, those dependencies have to be made explicit.

A blueprint breaks the argument into definitions and lemmas and shows how they fit together. That makes a large project easier to coordinate: people can work on different pieces while sharing a precise understanding of what each piece needs to establish. It also helps reveal missing steps before you invest too much effort in formalizing them.

But a blueprint isn’t itself a verified proof. It’s a roadmap that evolves as formalization exposes gaps or suggests better ways to organize the mathematics. Its value is in making that process visible and collaborative.

r001.rationale: The response says a blueprint lets people work on different pieces and coordinate, but it does not describe contributors claiming small tasks through it.
